title: Just Pay the Teachers?
author: Chad Aldeman
summary: Drawing on a new analysis of over 9,500 school districts he co-produced for The 74, Aldeman documents that American public schools have shed far fewer teaching staff than students — 11,000 fewer teachers against 225,000 fewer students in 2024-25 alone — a pattern he traces back decades using staffing-per-thousand-students data. A companion Missouri study calculates the opportunity cost directly: had the state held 2000-level staffing and redirected the savings to salaries, the average teacher would earn about $10,000 more today. Aldeman argues districts consistently choose to add administrative and support staff rather than raise teacher pay whenever budgets grow, a pattern he calls public education's 'Big Bet,' and that this happens not through deliberate anti-teacher decisions but because large organizations naturally find new things to spend money on once given more resources without productivity pressure. He closes by surveying policy levers — Arkansas's minimum salary floor, a New Jersey union-forced salary increase that was met by trimming other staff and class-size increases — arguing that only explicit mandates tying new funding directly to teacher pay reliably change the staffing-versus-salary tradeoff.
points: The core statistic — 11,000 fewer teachers against 225,000 fewer students in one year across 9,500-plus districts — quantifies a staffing-enrollment mismatch that undercuts the assumption that enrollment declines automatically translate into proportional staffing cuts.

The Missouri 'Personnel Boom' calculation (average teacher salary could be $10,000 higher, a 17% raise, had 2000-level staffing ratios been maintained) converts an abstract staffing trend into a concrete dollar cost borne by individual teachers.

Aldeman's explanation for the pattern — 'give an organization more resources without putting much pressure on it to become more productive, and it will find more things to do' — locates the cause in organizational incentive structure rather than any deliberate decision to underpay teachers.

The New Jersey case study (a union-forced salary increase funded by trimming other staff and slightly increasing class sizes, followed by measurable achievement gains) provides empirical evidence that forcing the staffing-to-salary tradeoff, rather than just adding money, is what changes district behavior.
quotes: In the latest year of data, the 2024-25 school year, the districts we examined employed 11,000 fewer teachers but served 225,000 fewer students. Going back to 2016-17, three-quarters of districts now have fewer students per teacher than they did eight years ago.

Frank and Koedel call this the "Personnel Boom," and they calculate its opportunity cost. If Missouri schools had simply maintained their 2000 staffing levels and redirected the savings toward teacher salaries, the average teacher could be earning about $10,000 more today, a 17% raise.
Whenever school spending goes up, schools don't raise teacher salaries. They don't extend the school year for students. They just add more staff.

When the first Baby Boomers started attending public schools in the 1950s, a typical American school district employed about 58 workers for every 1,000 students enrolled. By the time Millennials like myself attended school in the 1990s, schools employed twice as many adults to serve the same number of students.
Give an organization more resources without putting much pressure on it to become more productive, and it will find more things to do.

The short version here is that if policymakers want schools to spend more money on teacher salaries, they may have to make that choice for them, by setting higher salary floors or attaching new state funding directly to teacher pay.
